$comment: The single source of truth for every status claim in this repository.
README.md, docs/QUESTIONS.md, docs/ROADMAP.md and the marketing site all
render from this file via `mix ash_enterprise.roadmap`, which CI checks.
A status can therefore be wrong in one place only by being wrong in all of
them -- which is the point. Legal statuses: shipped | partial | planned | open.
shipped -- working code plus a test that would fail if it regressed.
partial -- works, with a named limitation stated in the answer.
planned -- an ADR and a plan exist, no code.
open    -- named as a gap, no decision taken.

sections.title: Who are you, and what may you do?
What happened, and can you prove it?
Where does data come from, and where does it go?
How does it change, and keep running?

questions.question: How do people prove who they are?
questions.answer: Password, magic link, OAuth2/OIDC and API keys via `ash_authentication`. No WebAuthn and no SAML anywhere in the ecosystem — the two gaps most likely to appear in an RFP.

questions.question: How is "may this actor do this?" decided?
questions.answer: `(role, privilege, depth)` rows evaluated as a pure union of grants — authorization is data, not code. No deny rules, so order cannot matter.

questions.question: Who owns a record?
questions.answer: Polymorphic user-or-team ownership inherited from the base resource. The Dataverse ownership type per entity is scraped from the corpus, never guessed.

questions.question: How does where you sit in the org chart change what you can see?
questions.answer: A business-unit tree with a materialized path, plus an optional manager/position hierarchy. Grant depth expands to a subtree once per request, never inside a policy check.

questions.question: Can one record be shared with someone the rules would not otherwise reach?
questions.answer: An `AccessGrant` row — Dataverse's `PrincipalObjectAccess` — adds rights to one record without widening any role.

questions.question: Are some columns more sensitive than the rows that contain them?
questions.answer: Not yet. Ash field policies would carry this on the same additive model, and the corpus already has `FieldPermission` and `FieldSecurityProfile` — but no field policy is declared anywhere in `lib/` today.

questions.question: Is every change recorded, including who and from where?
questions.answer: `AshEvents` writes a central append-only log on every create, update and destroy — inherited from the base resource, not wired per resource, so a new table cannot quietly have no history.

questions.question: Can you follow one request across the whole system at 3am?
questions.answer: One correlation id per request, stamped into audit metadata and OTel spans, and carried across process boundaries explicitly.

questions.question: Are illegal state transitions impossible, or merely discouraged?
questions.answer: `ash_state_machine` generates one named action per legal transition from the canonical Dataverse lifecycle. There is no generic `:update` that can set a state.

questions.question: Can a deletion be undone?
questions.answer: `ash_archival` soft delete, inherited. Opting out is an explicit `archival?: false` that a reviewer can grep for.

questions.question: Can you rebuild state by replaying the log?
questions.answer: The `AshEvents` replay machinery is wired, but the clear-records step deliberately refuses by default — it is indistinguishable from "delete all business data", so each deployment authorizes it explicitly.

questions.question: How are tenants separated?
questions.answer: Attribute multitenancy on `organization_id`, inherited by every resource — never schema-per-tenant, and never per-department.

questions.question: Does tenant isolation hold even when authorization is wrong?
questions.answer: Yes, and it is asserted as a separate property: the conformance suite checks isolation independently of every grant path.

questions.question: Can you erase a person on request?
questions.answer: No. `ash_archival` is soft delete only — there is no purge schedule, no anonymization pipeline, and an append-only audit log is exactly what a right-to-erasure request runs into.

questions.question: Where does the data physically live?
questions.answer: Undecided. Attribute multitenancy makes residency a deployment question rather than a schema one, which is a deferral, not an answer.

questions.question: How does data get in from systems you do not own?
questions.answer: Meltano lands rows in a staging schema as an external producer; a generator turns the declared target schema into an ordinary platform resource, so ingested data inherits ownership, tenancy and audit.

questions.question: How do you integrate N SaaS systems without writing N×M integrations?
questions.answer: One contract per category rather than one per (your app × their API). Nango holds the provider edge — OAuth, token refresh, the proxy — and the sync logic stays here as Ash actions over Oban, so a policy gates which actor may trigger a sync and the ordinary audit log records it. Nango's free self-hosted edition gates syncs and webhooks, which is why the design is split that way rather than generated wholesale.

questions.question: Can you trace a value back to the system it came from?
questions.answer: OpenLineage events whose run id *is* the correlation id the audit log already carries — lineage as a second consumer of existing telemetry rather than a parallel system. `ash_strangler` already ships the emitter for column-level mappings. Neither Meltano nor Airbyte emits OpenLineage, so the graph has a hole exactly where external data enters, and that is stated rather than drawn over.

questions.question: What data do you have, and who owns it?
questions.answer: A catalogue populated from codegen — every resource already declares its CDM provenance, ownership type and tenancy scope, so it is a read-only projection rather than a second source of truth. It is an internal tool only: its own RBAC resolves deny-wins, which is the inverse of this project's model.

questions.question: How do people get reports out of it?
questions.answer: Superset over views already filtered by the same actor context, so the BI tool's row-level security is a formality rather than a duplicate authorization model. Metabase loses because its RLS is paywalled.

questions.question: The same customer arrived from three systems — which one is real?
questions.answer: Entity resolution as an Ash calculation and change pipeline over the CDM-derived resources, so the golden record inherits ownership, audit and policy instead of living in a second system.

questions.question: How do you move onto this platform from a database you cannot stop?
questions.answer: `ash_strangler` maps a well-modelled resource onto the legacy schema through a closed grammar of typed combinators whose reverses are built rather than guessed, and moves it through four cutover phases without hand-written SQL. 341 tests, including round-trip properties over the legacy value space. **Running here**: `legacy.users` is read through a compatibility view as an ordinary platform resource, a Postgres trigger and listener make that surface live, and the same change is *projected* into a table this application owns -- so there are two live surfaces over the same people, one over the view and one over real columns, and the second is audited where the first structurally cannot be. Still partial, and deliberately: this is not a cutover. The legacy database remains the system of record, and the mapping is not invertible in two documented places (`full_name` cannot be split back into first and last; `company_id` is unmapped), which is exactly what a true cutover would have to resolve.

questions.question: How do the processes people actually follow get modelled?
questions.answer: `ash_bpmn` compiles a BPMN document into an immutable versioned graph and executes it with a token interpreter over Postgres and Oban, with an embedded designer. Gateway conditions are FEEL, the DMN expression language -- the hand-written expression evaluator it replaced is deleted. **Running here**: the six resources sit on the platform base resource, so a process instance is an ordinary owned, tenant-scoped record and the engine's bypass is the first policy in the base's own set. A published baseline, four seeded requests covering every branch of the gateway, and two tenants on different versions of the same key.

questions.question: How does an action get a second person's approval before it takes effect?
questions.answer: A change dropped on any action: work item, materialized candidate list, maker-checker exclusion applied by subtraction at candidate resolution rather than as a `forbid_if`, delegation, and escalation timers that get cancelled. **A work item is a platform resource here** -- owned, tenant-scoped and audited -- so who may approve is the same union of grants as who may read, and both the manager and executive approval branches are reachable in the demo. Still partial for one reason: nothing asserts that a user *without* the privilege cannot decide a task, and the positive case passing is not the same evidence.

questions.question: How do API contracts change without breaking the callers you cannot see?
questions.answer: Version deltas declared as data on the resource — one schema, N presentation contracts, no second table or view — with `render`/`parse` invertibility checked at compile time and sunset proposed from real traffic.

questions.question: How do you ship a change to some users first?
questions.answer: A flag is evaluated in-process against the application's own database, with actor, business unit and tenant supplied from the context already computed once per request. Policies are not a substitute — they answer *may you*, not *is this on*, and conflating them produces a `beta_user` role you then have to revoke from everyone.

questions.question: How does the schema itself evolve without drifting from the model?
questions.answer: Migrations are derived as a diff against committed resource snapshots, and the diff is a CI gate — so a resource change without a migration fails the build rather than surfacing at deploy time.

questions.question: Can you tell what is happening in production?
questions.answer: Correlation ids and Ash tracing are wired — `OpentelemetryAsh` is registered as the `Ash.Tracer`, so every action, query and calculation becomes a span with no per-resource wiring. Two things are not: `OpentelemetryPhoenix.setup/1` and `OpentelemetryEcto.setup/1` are never called, so those two declared dependencies emit nothing, and the OTLP endpoint the config comment says lives in `runtime.exs` is not there. The backend is now named; the bridge is still thin.

questions.question: How do enterprise customers bring their own identity provider?
questions.answer: Open. AshAuthentication ships password, magic link, API key and OAuth2, and no SAML — which is still the format most enterprise IdPs lead with in a procurement conversation. OIDC is reachable through the existing OAuth2 strategy; SAML would need a new one.

questions.question: How do accounts appear and disappear when someone joins or leaves?
questions.answer: Open. Users are created by registration and deactivated by a lifecycle transition; nothing consumes SCIM, so a customer removing someone from their directory does not remove them here.

questions.question: What second factor is required, and how are sessions bounded?
questions.answer: Open. Sessions are AshAuthentication's, with no MFA enforcement, no step-up for privileged actions and no configurable session lifetime. WebAuthn was named as a gap in thesis 7 and still is.

questions.question: Who may act as someone else, and is that recorded differently from acting as yourself?
questions.answer: Partial. Acting on someone else's behalf is now represented end to end: the record's `created_on_behalf_by_id` names the operator while `created_by_id` names the customer, and every audit event carries `impersonator_id`. What is missing is the gate — nothing yet decides who may impersonate whom, or records a session with a stated reason.

questions.question: Can the audit log be altered after the fact?
questions.answer: Shipped. Two mechanisms with different jobs: a trigger refuses `UPDATE` and `DELETE` outright, and every event carries a SHA-256 chained to the previous one, so an operator privileged enough to drop the trigger still cannot make an edit look untouched. `mix ash_enterprise.audit.verify` walks the chains; the suite proves it by tampering.

questions.question: Can a customer see their own audit trail, and only theirs?
questions.answer: Shipped. The log is attribute-multitenant on an `organization_id` the chain trigger derives from stamped metadata, so a tenant-scoped read is filtered by the data layer rather than by a policy written specially for the audit log. Depth answers how much of a tenant you see; tenancy answers which tenant.

questions.question: Can an auditor be handed a window of evidence without engineering help?
questions.answer: Shipped. `mix ash_enterprise.audit.export --from --to [--tenant]` writes CSV in chain order, including `sequence`, `previous_hash` and `hash` so the recipient can re-verify it rather than take it on trust. It reads through the ordinary action layer, so an export is exactly as wide as its requester's authorization.

questions.question: How long is evidence kept, and where does it live after ninety days?
questions.answer: Open. Nothing expires, nothing is partitioned, and nothing moves to cold storage — so a twelve-month SOC 2 observation window is retained by accident rather than by policy. Made sharper by the immutability trigger, which now actively refuses the `DELETE` a retention job would need.

questions.question: Are role and permission changes attributable to a person?
questions.answer: Shipped. Role assignments are ordinary audited resources, so granting one produces an event naming the grantor, the grantee and the correlation id of the request — and the record itself now carries `created_by_id`, which nothing populated before.

questions.question: Where do logs go to be reviewed, and what raises an alarm?
questions.answer: Open. Everything is queryable in Postgres and nothing streams anywhere. An auditor asks for evidence that logs are *reviewed*, not merely kept, and there is none: no SIEM export, no anomaly rules, no record of a human having looked.

questions.question: What crosses the tenant boundary, and to whom?
questions.answer: Open. There is no data inventory, no classification, and no published sub-processor list — which is the first artefact a security questionnaire asks for and the one that has to be current rather than merely written once.

questions.question: What does an AI model see, and can a customer opt out?
questions.answer: Partial. Thesis 5 settles the authorization half — an agent is an actor with an actor's permissions, and `ash_ai` tools are declarations that existing actions may be invoked, so a model reaches nothing its user could not. What is absent is the governance half: no prompt or response logging, no per-tenant opt-out, no disclosure of which model or vendor saw what.

questions.question: How do other systems find out that something happened here?
questions.answer: Open. Events land in the audit log and go nowhere else. There is no outbound webhook, no subscription, and no delivery guarantee for anyone who needs to react to a change rather than poll for it.

questions.question: How does a customer get fifty thousand rows in, or out?
questions.answer: Open. JSON:API and GraphQL paginate, and neither is a bulk path. Import exists only as a Meltano-shaped plan; export exists only for the audit log.

questions.question: Can a deploy happen without downtime, and can a migration be reversed?
questions.answer: Partial. Every generated migration has a `down`, and `ash_strangler`'s four-phase cutover is built precisely so a legacy migration can be reversed at any phase. What is untested is the app's own rolling deploy: nothing proves an old and a new node can serve the same schema at once, which is the property zero-downtime actually needs.

questions.question: Does it still work for a customer with fifty thousand of something?
questions.answer: Open. No load test, no query budget, and no pagination requirement on read actions — the audit export is the only place in the codebase that streams rather than loads. A reference architecture that has never met a large tenant is making an untested claim.

questions.question: Can a customer change how it behaves without a deploy?
questions.answer: Partial, and less partial than it was. A tenant can fork a process or a decision, edit it in the browser and publish it as its own version, with no binding row meaning 'follow the platform baseline' -- so changing behaviour is data, and reverting is deleting a row. Drift from a newer baseline is reported, never merged. What is still a deploy: adding an attribute is a resource change and a migration, and a decision cannot be tried against sample inputs before it is published.

questions.question: How are business rules expressed, versioned, and changed without a deploy?
questions.answer: As DMN decisions -- decision tables and literal expressions -- held as versioned, tenant-scoped Ash resources by `ash_decisions` and evaluated by a native Elixir DMN engine measured at 3,414 of 3,495 nodes against the official DMN TCK. Every evaluation records which version decided and what it saw. Partial: the resources and the engine are here, the authoring UI is not.

questions.question: Which named controls does any of this actually satisfy?
questions.answer: Partial. `docs/COMPLIANCE.md` maps SOC 2, ISO 27001 and GDPR controls to the questions above and through them to the test that proves each — generated from the same ledger, so it cannot drift. It covers technical prerequisites only: certification also needs policy, process and an auditor, and the document says so first rather than last.

questions.question: What is promised about uptime, and what happens when it is missed?
questions.answer: Open. No SLO, no error budget, no status page. Telemetry exists and nothing is expressed as a target, so there is nothing for an incident to be measured against.

questions.question: How quickly can you come back from losing the database?
questions.answer: Open. Backups are whatever the deployment provides; nothing here tests a restore, and an untested restore is a belief rather than a control. No RPO or RTO is committed to.

questions.question: When something breaks at three in the morning, what happens?
questions.answer: Open. Alerts go nowhere, no rota exists, and no runbook says who tells the customer. The correlation id makes the investigation possible; nothing makes it start.

questions.question: What is in the build, and can you prove nothing else is?
questions.answer: Partial. CI runs `mix hex.audit` for retired and vulnerable packages and `mix sobelow` for web vulnerabilities, and `mix.lock` pins everything transitively. There is no SBOM, no signed build, and no provenance attestation — so the dependency set is checked but not attested.

questions.question: Can you show a control operated continuously for twelve months?
questions.answer: Partial. This is the question the rest of the section is really asking. What exists: an unbroken, verifiable hash chain covering every write, exportable per tenant for any window. What does not: a retention policy guaranteeing the window is still there in month twelve, and any evidence that anyone reviewed it.

questions.question: How are business rules expressed, versioned and changed without a deploy?
questions.answer: As DMN, in `ash_decisions`. A decision is a DMN document -- the single artifact, with no second copy of the rules in a table to drift from it -- versioned and immutable on publish, edited in dmn-js, and evaluated either by a business rule task inside a process or by trigger routing deciding which process to start. The engine is adopted rather than written and measured at 97.68% of the official DMN TCK. `OUTPUT ORDER` and `RULE ORDER` are refused at compile time because both make document order semantically significant, which is the same order-dependence the authorization model rejects. What is missing is the proof: publish-time overlap and completeness analysis is designed and unbuilt, so a table with a gap or an overlap publishes without complaint.

questions.question: Can a UI built on the new model be driven by a database the old application still owns?
questions.answer: Yes, and it is demonstrated rather than asserted: `INSERT INTO legacy.users` in `psql` reaches a surface generated from `AshEnterprise.Accounts.ProjectedUser` -- an Ash-owned table with real columns -- without a reload and without anything in that surface knowing a legacy database exists. The chain is an `AFTER` trigger, `pg_notify` on commit, a listener that re-reads through Ash so the mapped values apply, a notifier that upserts through an ordinary Ash action, and `Ash.Notifier.PubSub`. What it costs: the projection is eventually consistent, and `projected_at` is a column so the lag is on screen rather than hidden. A row that fails to project is silently absent until the backfill is re-run -- there is no retry, and the reconciliation job that would close that gap is not built.

items.title: Legacy migration, process modelling and decisions as platform extensions
items.choice: ash_strangler + ash_bpmn + ash_decisions, first-party
items.effort: Three packages at 0.1.0 under MIT with substantial suites -- 341 tests for the strangler, 198 for BPMN, 101 plus a 3,495-assertion conformance corpus for decisions. The composition is what was outstanding and is now done: all three are dependencies, their resources sit on this application's base resource, a process runs here end to end, and the legacy estate is both read live through a view and projected into a table this application owns.
items.bar: Yes for both, now. `ash_strangler` by construction — its output is read through the ordinary action layer. `ash_bpmn` because a work item on `AshEnterprise.Platform.Resource` inherits this policy set, with one ordering rule: Ash's bypasses skip only the policies declared after them, so the engine's bypass has to sit at the top of `AshEnterprise.Security.Policies` or the engine acts as a `SystemActor` this set already admits.
items.answer: All three are dependencies of this application and their resources are this application's own: a legacy table is mapped and read here, and the process, decision and trigger tables inherit `AshEnterprise.Platform.Resource` -- so an instance is an ordinary owned, tenant-scoped, audited record and the engines' authority is two declared policy bypasses rather than an option at a call site. Demonstrated rather than asserted: an `AccessRequest` submission is one audited write, a trigger matches it, a FEEL guard filters it, a DMN decision routes it, and four seeded requests drive all three branches of the gateway. What is not here is a FEEL editor, and decision evaluation from the editor.

items.title: Data ingestion
items.choice: Meltano (MIT); Airbyte as the fallback
items.effort: A `mix meltano.gen.resource` mirroring the CDM generator, carrying its refusals across: ownership is never guessed and foreign keys are never invented. Promotion out of the staging schema is an ordinary Ash action — the only place ingested data acquires ownership, tenancy and audit.
items.bar: No, by refusal: Meltano is kept outside the boundary where authorization applies, so there is no second model to synchronize. The cost is that staging rows are unauthorized at rest, and a pipeline landing two tenants into one table is a defect the platform cannot detect.

items.title: Integration hub — avoiding M×N
items.choice: Nango for the provider edge only
items.effort: Verification inverted the design: Nango's free self-hosted edition covers auth and proxy but gates syncs, actions and webhooks, so generating an action per Nango sync would put the mechanism behind a paid tier. Nango holds the provider edge; sync logic stays here as Ash actions over Oban.
items.bar: Yes, with one load-bearing rule: the Nango connection id is never an action argument — it is derived from the actor's tenant. Otherwise the policy engine authorizes the operation while the caller picks whose credentials to spend. The residual is stated, not wrapped away: anyone holding the Nango secret key bypasses every policy.

items.title: Lineage and provenance
items.choice: OpenLineage + Marquez
items.effort: A notifier whose OpenLineage `runId` *is* the existing correlation id and whose parent facet derives from the existing depth counter. It runs inside the action, after authorization, so lineage records authorized effects rather than a privileged crawl. `ash_strangler` already ships a columnLineage emitter.
items.bar: Marquez has no authorization model at all — which forces two rules: deploy it like `clarity`, behind the same boundary, and never put a value, actor or tenant into a facet. No verifier enforces the second.

items.title: Approvals and maker-checker
items.choice: ash_bpmn — no external engine
items.effort: Built and tested in the package, including duplicate refusal via a partial unique index and timer cancellation, and now running here: a manager approval and an executive approval are both reachable from the seeded demo and both appear on `/app/tasks` behind the actor's principal ids. Remaining, and the reason this is not shipped: no test asserts the *negative* -- that a user without the privilege cannot decide a task -- which is this file's own bar.
items.bar: The decisive argument against Camunda or Flowable — an external engine is a second authorization and data model to keep in sync, and it would express maker-checker as a deny rule, which this repository forbids.
items.answer: `ash_bpmn` adopted, with its work item on the platform base resource and the engine's authority declared as the first bypass in the base's policy set rather than as an option at a call site. Maker-checker is applied by subtraction at candidate resolution, never as a `forbid_if`. Decisions a process routes on are `ash_decisions`. A process runs here and people can complete its tasks; what is still missing is the test that would fail if the wrong person could.

items.title: Business rules and decision tables
items.choice: ash_decisions — DMN, engine adopted not written
items.effort: A first-party package over `boxic_dmn`/`boxic_feel`: versioned immutable definitions, tenancy, the authorization bypass, the evaluation log, the dmn-js editor, and an independent run of the official DMN TCK as the gate. 101 tests plus 3,495 corpus assertions.
items.bar: The measurement, not the preference. Writing a conforming FEEL implementation is a 60–90 person-day project; an independent TCK run put the existing engine at 97.68% before any work of ours, so it was adopted. What makes a 0.x package by one author defensible is that it sits behind a single adapter module and the conformance suite is ours — replacing it is measurable rather than speculative.
items.answer: DMN, as its own first-party package. The DMN document is the single artifact — no second copy of the rules in a table — versioned per tenant, evaluated by a business rule task or by trigger routing, and edited in dmn-js. **97.68% of the official DMN TCK** (3,414 of 3,495 asserted result nodes; level 2 96.83%, level 3 97.71%), with each remaining failure listed against a measured node count so the gate fails if it moves in either direction. Not shipped: publish-time overlap and completeness analysis, which is designed and unbuilt; no way to evaluate a decision from the editor; and `matched_rule_ids` is always empty because the engine reports what a decision returned but not which rule produced it.

items.title: Data catalog and governance
items.choice: OpenMetadata (DataHub is the closer call it looks)
items.effort: A push step alongside `mix ash.codegen`, writing each resource's declared metadata over the REST API as a bot. Two stateful services, not one: OpenMetadata requires Elasticsearch or OpenSearch as well as Postgres.
items.bar: The least comfortable answer of the set. OpenMetadata's RBAC has Allow/Deny rules where deny wins — the exact inverse of a pure union — so no attempt is made to mirror roles into it, and the catalogue can therefore never face tenants.

items.title: Reporting and embedded analytics
items.choice: Apache Superset over Metabase
items.effort: Tenant- and role-scoped views generated from the existing actor context, so Superset's own RLS config is a formality.
items.bar: The deciding factor. Metabase paywalls row-level security even when self-hosted, which would put this project's central thesis behind a paywall.

items.title: API versioning and deprecation
items.choice: ash_api_versioning
items.effort: A new extension. No new database objects — that property is what makes it categorically cheaper than the strangler, and losing it makes it pointless.
items.bar: Not applicable — this is ours, and it wraps the action layer rather than bypassing it.

items.title: Feature flags and progressive delivery
items.choice: FunWithFlags (Unleash rejected)
items.effort: Protocol implementations declared once, so actor, business unit and tenant become flag targeting for free. Verification reversed the expected answer twice over: the widely-cited Unleash end-of-life attaches to Edge OSS rather than the server, but the server relicensed Apache-2.0 to AGPL-3.0 at v8.0.0 and its OSS edition is capped at one project and two environments.
items.bar: Unleash fails on a fact worse than licensing: its Elixir SDK is community-maintained and silently ignores segments and flag dependencies, so a flag the Unleash UI says excludes a user returns true for them. FunWithFlags evaluates in-process against the application's own Postgres.

items.title: Observability backend
items.choice: Grafana LGTM
items.effort: Close to zero Ash-side work — the exporters exist and need a destination. Three concrete follow-ups came out of checking rather than assuming: call the Phoenix and Ecto setup functions, put the OTLP endpoint where the config comment claims it is, and note that Grafana Agent and Promtail reached end of life on 2025-11-01.
items.bar: Not applicable — telemetry is not an authorization surface. The licence mix is the interesting part: the collection tier (Alloy) is Apache-2.0 while the storage tier is copyleft.

items.title: Master data and entity resolution
items.choice: In-Ash resolution over CDM resources
items.effort: The golden-record shape is adopted rather than invented: the vendored `Account` and `Contact` CDM entities already carry `merged` and a self-referencing `master`/`masterid`. Match, merge and survivorship become ordinary changes and calculations.
items.bar: A golden record inside the platform inherits ownership, audit and policy. Two consequences fall out that an external hub hides: candidate generation must run as a system actor, so the review queue can leak the existence of duplicates; and a merge can revoke a user's access without revoking any grant, because grants are per-record and the record moved. AtroCore is GPL-3.0, not the MIT its own marketing claims; Pimcore left open source entirely in 2025.

items.title: Audit retention, partitioning and erasure
items.choice: Time-partitioned hot/cold split; erasure by crypto-shredding
items.effort: Monthly partitions on `audit_events`, ninety days hot, the rest detached to cheaper storage and still chain-verifiable. The hard half is not partitioning: it is that erasure and an append-only log are in direct conflict, and the resolution has to preserve the chain — which points at encrypting subject data per person and destroying the key rather than deleting rows.
items.bar: No external tool. Retention is a property of the log, and the log is the thing this platform's audit story rests on — handing it to something outside the boundary would put the evidence chain outside it too.

items.title: Control mapping and evidence
items.choice: Generated from the ledger; SOC 2, ISO 27001, GDPR
items.effort: `docs/controls.json` maps control ids to ledger questions and their proofs, rendered into `docs/COMPLIANCE.md` and the site by the same task that renders the roadmap. Remaining: the evidence-of-review half, which needs the SIEM item, and per-control screenshots an auditor can be handed.
items.bar: The map claims technical prerequisites and says so in its first paragraph. Claiming more would make the honesty mechanism the rest of this repository is built on worthless.

items.title: Enterprise identity: SAML, OIDC and SCIM
items.choice: AshAuthentication strategies; SCIM as a resource-backed endpoint
items.effort: OIDC through the existing OAuth2 strategy is small. SAML needs a new strategy and an XML signature story. SCIM is the larger piece and the more interesting one here: provisioning maps onto ordinary create and lifecycle actions, so it is an endpoint over existing actions rather than a parallel user store.
items.bar: Yes. An identity provider authenticates; it never authorizes. Group-to-role mapping stays here as `(role, privilege, depth)` rows, which is the difference between an IdP telling us who you are and an IdP telling us what you may do.

items.title: Break-glass and impersonation control
items.choice: In-Ash: a session resource with a stated reason
items.effort: Attribution shipped — records and events name both the customer and the operator. Remaining: a session resource carrying who, whom, when, why and for how long; a privilege gating it; and a notification to the account owner, which is the control customers actually ask for.
items.bar: No external tool. Who may act as whom is an authorization question, and this platform already has exactly one place authorization is expressed.

items.title: Log shipping, review and alerting
items.choice: Structured export to the customer's SIEM; Grafana for ours
items.effort: A notifier streaming audit events as structured JSON to a customer-configured sink, per tenant, with the chain hashes intact so the copy is verifiable against the original. Alerting rules follow the same ledger the control map does.
items.bar: Partial by design: a SIEM cannot consume ActorContext, so the boundary is that it receives only what one tenant is entitled to and never a cross-tenant stream.

items.title: SLOs, disaster recovery and incident response
items.choice: Committed RPO/RTO with a tested restore; error budgets
items.effort: A restore drill in CI against a real dump is the load-bearing piece — an untested backup is a belief. SLOs and error budgets sit on the telemetry that already exists; the status page and rota are process rather than code, and are named as such.
items.bar: Not applicable in the usual sense, and worth saying so: these are operational commitments, not tools with authorization models. The bar they have to clear is that they are tested rather than asserted.

items.title: Outbound events and subscriptions
items.choice: An Ash notifier over the existing event log
items.effort: The audit log already contains every change with an actor and a tenant. A subscription is a filtered, tenant-scoped view of it with delivery and retry — which is Oban's job, not a new event system's.
items.bar: Yes, and unusually cleanly: a subscription is a read, so it is filtered by the same policies as any other read. A customer cannot subscribe to what they cannot see.

items.title: Bulk import and export
items.choice: Ash bulk actions over a staged upload
items.effort: `Ash.bulk_create` and `Ash.bulk_update` already exist and are authorized per record. The work is the staging surface, the error report a user can act on, and streaming exports that do not load a tenant into memory — the audit export is the pattern.
items.bar: Yes. Bulk is the same actions in a loop, so ownership, tenancy and audit apply per row rather than being skipped for speed.

items.title: Data inventory, classification and sub-processors
items.choice: Derived from resource metadata, not maintained by hand
items.effort: Every resource already declares its CDM provenance, ownership type and tenancy scope. Classification is one more declaration, and the inventory is then generated — the same argument as the control map, and the same reason it will still be true in a year.
items.bar: Overlaps the catalog item deliberately: this is the compliance artefact, that is the discovery tool, and both should read from the same declarations.

items.title: SBOM and build provenance
items.choice: CycloneDX SBOM; attested builds
items.effort: An SBOM generated in CI and attached to each release, plus provenance attestation for the container. Small, mechanical, and asked about on every enterprise security questionnaire.
items.bar: Not applicable — nothing here touches the authorization model. It is on the list because it is asked for, and off priority 1 because nothing depends on it.

items.title: Zero-downtime deploys and reversible migrations
items.choice: Expand/contract, proven by a two-version test
items.effort: Every migration already has a `down`. What is missing is a test that an old and a new node can serve the same schema simultaneously, which is what zero-downtime actually requires and what `down` alone does not give.
items.bar: Not applicable. Named because 'reversible migrations' is on every enterprise checklist and this repository can currently only claim half of it.

items.title: Performance at enterprise data volumes
items.choice: A seeded large tenant and a query budget
items.effort: Seed a tenant with fifty thousand of the widest resource, then assert query counts and response times in CI. The interesting result is not the number; it is which of the inherited policies turn out to cost something at that size.
items.bar: Not applicable, but load-bearing for thesis 3: an authorization model that is elegant and slow is not a model anyone keeps.

items.title: AI governance: what leaves the tenant boundary
items.choice: Prompt/response logging as audit events; per-tenant opt-out
items.effort: Thesis 5 already did the hard part — an agent is an actor, so a model reaches nothing its user could not, and there is no agent-specific authorization path to secure. What is left is disclosure: log prompt and response as audit events under the same tenant and correlation id as the action they produced, record which model and vendor saw them, and let a tenant switch the whole thing off.
items.bar: Yes, and it is the clearest case in the set. An LLM provider is a service behind a network boundary that cannot consume ActorContext, so the rule from thesis 6 applies literally: it receives only what one actor was already entitled to, and removing it degrades a feature rather than breaking the app.
